title: Private deployments: VPC & on‑prem deployment guide, packaging, day‑2 ops, and upgrade/rollback procedures
author: Ava Chen
body:
Overview

Purpose: This guide consolidates Redwood Inference best practices for private deployments (VPC and on‑prem) covering reference architectures, packaging requirements, customer pre‑deployment checklist, day‑2 operational procedures, and robust upgrade/rollback playbooks. Target audience: Solutions engineers, SREs, and customer ops teams responsible for onboarding and operating Private deployments.

Contents
1) Summary and reference architectures
2) On‑prem packaging and delivery checklist
3) Customer requirements library (network, security, capacity)
4) Day‑2 operations: monitoring, backups, incident playbooks
5) Upgrade and rollback procedures (safe rollout patterns)
6) Ownership, SLAs, and runbook links

1) Summary and reference architectures
- Supported modes: VPC (cloud-hosted private control plane), Air‑gapped on‑prem appliance, Hybrid (control plane in customer VPC + on‑prem runtime).
- Key design goals: data isolation, predictable latency, and easy upgrades.
- Primary components: Control plane (Redwood control services), Runtime cluster (K8s or bare‑metal GPU nodes), Ingress/proxy (Envoy/NGINX), Storage (object store or NFS), Key management (KMS/HSM), Telemetry forwarding (Prometheus, Jaeger)

Recommended minimal topology (single AZ proof‑of‑concept):
| Component | Recommended instance | Notes |
| Control plane | m5.large equivalent (cloud) / VM for on‑prem | Runs API gateway, RBAC, management UI |
| Runtime nodes | 1‑4 GPU servers (A100/RTX6000) | Model serving containers, auto‑scale as needed |
| Storage | S3/GCS or MinIO | Model artifacts and KV cache persistency |
| Networking | Private subnet, NAT, VPN/Direct Connect | Customer must enable outbound to control plane endpoints (unless fully air‑gapped) |

2) On‑prem packaging and delivery checklist
Pre‑delivery: confirm customer requirements, sign off on network and security documents, and schedule maintenance window.
Packaging contents:
- Installer bundle (versioned tarball) with checksums and SBOM
- Kubernetes manifests + Helm charts (if using K8s) or systemd units for bare‑metal
- Container images (registry or offline tarballs)
- Deployment guide (this document + site‑specific addendum)
- License and keys (customer HSM/KMS instructions)
- Troubleshooting quickstart and healthcheck script

Installer validation steps (post‑install):
1. run ./healthcheck.sh -> must return: all-services: OK
2. prometheus scrape targets >= expected node count
3. sample inference request against local gateway -> 200 OK, latency <= target

3) Customer requirements library (network, security, capacity)
Minimum network requirements:
- CIDR allocations for control and runtime subnets
- Ports: 443 (API), 2181‑2199 (internal cluster ports), 9090 (Prometheus), 9411 (Zipkin/Jaeger) — full list provided in appendix A
- VPN or Direct Connect for control plane connectivity (unless air‑gapped)

Security & compliance requirements:
- Customer-managed KMS recommended for model encryption keys
- Audit logging: all admin actions must be forwarded to centralized SIEM (syslog/CEF)
- RBAC: integrate with SSO (SAML/OIDC) — service account provisioning steps included

Capacity & sizing guidance:
- Small POC: 1 GPU (NVIDIA T4 or equivalent), 2 CPU control plane VMs, 500GB storage
- Production baseline: 4 GPUs (A100/80GB preferred), 3 control plane nodes (HA), 5TB storage (models + cache), 99.9% uptime target
- Batching & KV cache footprint: estimate 1‑2GB per active model per node

4) Day‑2 operations: monitoring, backups, and common procedures
Monitoring & alerting:
- Default SLOs: 99.9% node availability, 95th percentile tail latency per model <= customer SLA (configurable per deployment)
- Prometheus alert rules (examples):
  - Node down -> P1
  - Model queue backlog > 500 reqs -> P2
  - KV cache hit rate < 60% for 30m -> investigate model config
- Dashboards: per‑model latency, per‑node GPU utilization, per‑tenant cost breakdown (if multi‑tenant)

Backup & restore:
- Daily snapshot of metadata DB (encrypted) and weekly object store snapshot
- Restore procedure (high level): 1) Shut down runtime ingress 2) Restore DB snapshot 3) Rehydrate model artifacts to storage 4) Start control plane -> run healthcheck

Operational playbooks (short):
- Model serving failure: check container logs -> restart pod -> if N+1 failures, roll back to previous model version and notify customer
- Disk pressure: drain node, cordon, free cached model artifacts, re‑add node after clean up

5) Upgrade and rollback procedures (safe rollout patterns)
Principles: run upgrades in non‑peak windows, use canary and automated health gating, maintain rollback artifacts and runbook.
Upgrade types:
- Control plane patch (config or minor version): rolling upgrade, 1 node at a time, health check between nodes
- Runtime (model serving) version upgrade: canary traffic to 5% of capacity for 30 minutes, metric gate: error rate increase <= 1% and p95 latency delta <= +20%
- Major version (runtime + control plane): do staged upgrade: staging -> canary -> region -> global

Step‑by‑step: Runtime canary example
1. Build and publish candidate images to customer registry (or provide tarball).
2. Deploy canary with label canary=true to 1 GPU node set (5% capacity).
3. Route 5% production traffic using traffic‑split rule in envoy/ingress.
4. Monitor for 30 minutes using automation (alerts suppressed for known noise):
   - error rate, latency, resource usage, KV cache hit rate
5. If pass metrics, increment to 25% -> 50% -> 100% with 15‑30m gates.
6. If at any gate an alert crosses threshold, execute rollback: run kubectl rollout undo or replace images with previous digest and reverify healthcheck.

Rollback playbook (quick):
- Abort traffic migration, cut traffic to stable pool, restore previous image digest from registry, rehydrate cached model artifacts if missing, run healthcheck, notify customer and internal stakeholders.

6) Ownership, SLAs, runbooks and links
- Deployment owner: Solutions Engineering (primary), Eng‑SRE (oncall for infra), Customer Success (customer escalation)
- Escalation path: oncall -> eng‑sre -> runtime team -> oncall lead -> exec oncall (contact matrix in appendix B)
- Runbooks: link to specific runbooks for incident types (model OOM, network partition, audit log failure)

Appendices
A) Full port and endpoint list (text table)
B) Escalation contact matrix and oncall rotation (roles and pager duties)
C) Example CLI snippets

Example CLI snippets
- Healthcheck:
  curl -sSf https://localhost:443/health | jq '.'
- Canary rollout (K8s):
  kubectl apply -f deployment-canary.yaml --record
  kubectl set image deployment/runtime runtime=registry.example.com/redwood/runtime:v1.2.3-canary
